title: infra-gpu-fleet-capacity-cloud-accounts-iac-ci-cd-playbook-2026-addendum
author: Aisha Patel
content:
Summary

This playbook is an operational addendum (2026) for Redwood Inference infrastructure teams covering GPU fleet and capacity planning, cloud accounts and networking patterns, Terraform/IaC module guidelines, and CI/CD/build pipelines. It consolidates best practices, runbooks, and actionable checklists for day-to-day operations and project onboarding. This doc is intended for infra engineers, SREs, and platform owners responsible for provisioning, scaling, and operating GPU-backed inference capacity.

Scope

- GPU fleet sizing, headroom targets, and allocation strategies across hosted/dedicated/private modes.
- Cloud account structure, network topology, and cross-account access patterns.
- Terraform/IaC module design, versioning, and testing requirements.
- CI/CD pipelines for infra modules, GPU image builds, and deployment promotion.
- Runbooks for capacity incidents, planned scale events, and rollback procedures.

Ownership and Contacts

- Primary owner: infra-capacity (engineering)
- Secondary owner: serving-runtime (engineering)
- Oncall escalation: infra-oncall -> infra-sre -> platform-eng lead
- Pager duty runbook: infra-gpu-capacity-pager (see runbooks section)

High-level Goals and SLOs

- 99.9% provisioning success for new GPU node pools within target window (SLO window: 30 minutes for hot capacity, 4 hours for cold).
- Maintain 25% fleet spare capacity headroom for Dedicated to absorb traffic spikes and rolling upgrades.
- Max median model startup latency increase during scale events: 10% over baseline.
- Terraform drift detection: surface drift within 10 minutes of change detection and create an alert.

GPU Fleet and Capacity Strategy

1) Fleet composition and labels

- Fleet groups: hosted-general, dedicated-highmem, private-onprem.
- Label metadata: workload (low-latency, batch), memory_profile (standard, highmem), quant_profile (fp16, int8).
- Hardware mix guidance: prefer uniform families per pool (e.g., A100-40GB in dedicated-highmem) to simplify kernel optimization and scheduling.

2) Headroom and scaling policy

- Target steady-state headroom: 25% for Dedicated, 15% for Hosted.
- Autoscaling tiers:
  1. Fast autoscaler (latency-sensitive queues): scale within 2-5 minutes.
  2. Bulk autoscaler (batch/embeddings): scale within 15-30 minutes.
  3. Cold-provisioning (private/on-prem extra capacity): scale within 2-6 hours.
- Bump policy for planned events: add a 20% temporary buffer 24 hours before large model release or marketing-driven traffic.

3) Allocation and reservation

- Reservation rules: customer commitments for Dedicated are backed by reserved node pools with capacity floor and eviction protection.
- Preemption policy: Hosted best-effort pools may use preemptible instances with graceful eviction: 5-minute drain window for in-flight requests and checkpoint KV caches.

Cloud Accounts and Networking

1) Account structure

- Prod accounts: prod-us-west-2, prod-eu-west-1 (one per region).
- Shared infra accounts: infra-platform (for centralized networking, VPN, landing zones), infra-ci (for CI runners and build artifacts).
- Customer-dedicated: per-customer dedicated AWS/GCP account or VPC as contractually required.

2) Networking model

- VPC layout: public control plane subnets (load balancers), private compute subnets (GPU nodes), and transit subnet for inter-region replication.
- Transit & peering: use Transit Gateway (or equivalent) for multi-account connectivity; avoid full-mesh peering.
- Egress controls: centralized NAT gateways per AZ for cost predictability.

3) Security & connectivity

- Cross-account roles: least-privilege IAM roles for infra automation (CI deploy pipelines assume-role into target account).
- KMS/HSM: customer-managed CMKs for Private deployments; use envelope encryption for runtime secrets.
- Bastion and jump hosts: restrict to approved IP ranges and MFA.

Terraform / IaC Module Guidelines

1) Module boundaries and semantics

- Keep modules focused: network, compute-gpu-pool, iam-roles, monitoring, and ci-runners. Each module must have a README with inputs, outputs, examples, and constraints.
- No cross-module resource ownership: modules should reference outputs from a single source-of-truth module to avoid drift.

2) Versioning and releases

- Semantic versioning on module registries (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH).
- Release process: merge -> CI tests -> publish module artifact -> tag and update consuming stacks in a PR.

3) Testing and validation

- Mandatory tests for all modules: unit plan tests (terraform plan with -target stubs), integration apply in ephemeral accounts (destroy after test), and policy checks (tfsec/OPA).
- Automated drift detection: run terraform plan in infra-monitoring every 5-15 minutes for critical stacks and create alerts on drift.

4) State management

- Remote state: use centralized S3/GCS backend with state locking (DynamoDB/Cloud Storage locks).
- State access: restrict to automation roles and per-team service accounts; audits pushed to log archive account.

CI/CD and Build Pipelines

1) Pipeline taxonomy

- Module CI: lint -> unit-plan -> acceptance (ephemeral apply) -> publish artifacts.
- Infra stack CD: PR -> plan -> approval gates -> apply in non-prod -> canary -> apply in prod.
- GPU image pipeline: base image build -> model runtime bake -> security + performance tests -> push to registry.

2) Pipeline requirements

- All infra PRs must include a terraform plan artifact and cost estimate (terraform-cost-estimator).
- Canary policy for pool scaling changes: stage change to 10% of targeted pools, wait 30 minutes, evaluate error and latency metrics, then proceed.
- Roll-forward rule: automatic rollback on >5% increase in error rate or breach of SLO during canary window.

3) CI runner sizing and isolation

- Runners for module acceptance tests should be in infra-ci account with ephemeral instances sized for parallel acceptance (8-16 vCPUs, 64-128GB RAM) depending on test profile.
- Sensitive credentials: delivered via short-lived OIDC tokens; avoid long-lived secrets in runner images.

Runbooks and Operational Playbooks

1) Capacity incident runbook (high-level)

- Trigger: steady increase in queuing latency beyond 95th percentile threshold for 5 minutes or an autoscaler failure.
- Immediate steps:
  1. Triage: check autoscaler, cluster metrics, and infra-controller logs.
  2. If autoscaler blocked: attempt manual scale of targeted pool +1x and monitor.
  3. If manual scale fails: open incident, page infra-oncall, and create a short-lived hot pool from pre-built AMI.
  4. Notify product and customer-success if customer-dedicated capacity is affected.
- Post-incident: run root-cause analysis (RCA) and update capacity forecasts.

2) Planned capacity increase checklist

- Pre-checks (48-24 hours): validate terraform plan in staging, ensure image compatibility, confirm network quotas (ENIs, IPs), and notify oncall.
- Execution (T-24 to T+24): create reservation, expand pool in staging canary, validate latency and error metrics for 1 hour, then roll to prod in 20% increments with 30-minute observation windows.
- Rollback criteria: increased 95th latency >15% or error rate >2x baseline for 30 minutes.

3) Kernel/driver upgrade procedure

- Stage: bake test AMI with new driver and collect perf regressions using benchmark suite.
- Canary: roll to 5% of nodes (non-dedicated) and validate KV cache warmup and model perf.
- Full rollout: incrementally update pools with drain-and-replace, monitor model-level latency and tail latencies.

Operational Metrics and Dashboards

- Required dashboards: GPU utilization (avg / p95), queue depth by pool, autoscaler health, terraform drift alerts, image bake success rate, and build pipeline failure rate.
- Key alerts and thresholds:
  - Queue depth > configured threshold for 5 minutes -> P1 alert.
  - Autoscaler error rate > 1 per hour -> P2 alert.
  - Terraform drift detected for prod core stacks -> P1 alert.

Change Management and Runbook Updates

- All changes to this playbook must be made via PR in the infra-team-docs repo and reviewed by at least two reviewers including an SRE and a runtime owner.
- Quarterly review cadence: schedule a playbook review (Q1/Q2/Q3/Q4) and reconcile with postmortem action items.

Appendices

A) Example terraform module header (README excerpt)

- Name: compute-gpu-pool
- Purpose: create an autoscaling GPU node pool with node labels, taints, and lifecycle hooks.
- Inputs (example): region, instance_type, min_size, max_size, node_labels (map), taints (list).
- Outputs (example): node_pool_id, autoscaling_group_arn, instance_profile.

B) Quick CLI snippets

- Manual scale example:
  aws autoscaling set-desired-capacity --auto-scaling-group-name <name> --desired-capacity <n> --region <region>

- Terraform plan with targeted check:
  terraform init && terraform plan -target=module.compute-gpu-pool

C) Useful links

- Infra runbooks: /confluence/eng-infra/runbooks
- Terraform module registry: internal-module-registry.redwood.local
- Capacity forecast spreadsheet: drive/redwood-inference/infra/capacity-forecasts
